A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UltraEdit and UltraEditBench. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding algorithms, equations, tables, and figures can be matched despite reformatting and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original editing experiments, normalization ablations, scalability measurements, and downstream capability evaluations in Sections 4–5 and Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and reports additional UnKE results, semantic-judge evaluations, dataset analyses, and two-million-edit results.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the proposed procedure are unchanged: hidden-state/gradient features, lifelong normalization, norm-based scaling, and regularized least-squares parameter updates. Rewritten explanations and newly documented evaluation settings do not establish an algorithm change.

E1.justification: v2 adds unstructured long-text editing on UnKE, supplemented with AKEW examples for unrelated-knowledge evaluation. This extends coverage beyond v1's four editing benchmarks. The original editing datasets and downstream capability tasks remain.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is retained in matched experiments, including the extended appendix comparisons. The new UnKE and judge evaluations use existing FT, WISE, AlphaEdit, and RLEdit comparators. Newly mentioned MoKE and SMEdit are explicitly excluded, not evaluated.

E3.justification: The reported UltraEditBench large-scale setting increases from 1M to 2M edits. New UnKE experiments introduce 500-edit comparisons and 1,000-edit UltraEdit rows with BERTScore and ROUGE-L. v2 also adds complementary DeepSeek-V3.1 judging with a specified prompt and 512-token output limit.

E4.justification: v2 adds benchmark diversity analyses covering domains, subject languages, answer lengths, and lexical statistics, plus a complementary semantic-evaluation check. Existing scalability analyses extend to 2M edits. The normalization ablations in Table 4 and the case-study examples remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Averaging across backbone models already appears in v1; v2's edit-order-insensitivity statement supplies no new statistical estimation procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds UnKE and judge results; for example, Table 13 reports LLaMA-3 judge efficacy of 52.85 for UltraEdit versus 58.47 for AlphaEdit. Table 3 replaces 1M-edit results with 2M-edit results, including GPT-J specificity changing from 74.96 to 76.44. These have different edit counts, not a same-setting performance gain. Tables 2 and 4 retain their numerical results.

T1.justification: The editing definitions, running-statistic equations, objective, and closed-form solution remain unchanged. The added BERTScore and ROUGE-L formulas explain adopted evaluation metrics; no new theoretical result, proof, or changed mathematical reasoning is introduced.

C1.justification: The headline scalability claim rises from 1M to 2M edits, and the claimed VRAM requirement strengthens from less than one-third to less than one-quarter of prior methods. Claimed empirical support expands to five editing datasets and complementary judging, while the original four contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly connects normalization to mitigating internal covariate shift and knowledge overwriting, and clarifies applicability without future edits. Section 5.3 newly concludes that UltraEdit does not increase hallucination risk, although its underlying capability tests are unchanged. The computational-resource limitation is retained.

D1.justification: New documentation specifies evaluation after all edits, distinct samples, and a common editing order. v2 supplies the judge prompt, model and output limit, UnKE/AKEW assembly details, UnKE editable modules, and WISE training-set information. These substantially expand reproducibility information; existing hardware, learning rate, and code/data links remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds references concerning AKEW, evaluation in the wild, DeepSeek, MoKE, and SMEdit, while removing several earlier citations. Table 1 and Section 2.2 revise memory-based methods' classification from training-free to requiring training. The basic positioning against three editing paradigms remains.

P1.justification: Substantial passages in the abstract, introduction, method motivation and explanation, and analysis are rewritten or condensed. v2 adds a reproducibility section and reorganizes the appendix around additional statements. Title, authorship, terminology, and citation style also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds diversity, judge-prompt, UnKE, and judge-result tables, expands the module-settings table, and redistributes existing tables. Figures 5 and 8 are redrawn with revised axes and 2M endpoints. The document template, headers, typography, and float placement change throughout; other figures are retained.

improvement.justification: Long-text testing, complementary semantic judging, and clearer evaluation documentation make v2 more informative and reproducible. The gain is limited by insufficient discussion of adverse results, including Mistral's UnKE efficacy falling from 92.94 at 500 edits to 62.79 at 1,000 edits. v2 also strengthens its VRAM claim despite unchanged Figure 2 and adds a hallucination-risk assurance unsupported by the retained capability tests. The added evidence improves assessability, but these overstatements prevent a stronger overall improvement.
